definition: A residual neural network (also referred to as a residual network or ResNet) is a deep learning architecture in which the layers learn residual functions with reference to the layer inputs.
details: It was developed in 2015 for image recognition, and won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) of that year. As a point of terminology, "residual connection" refers to the specific architectural motif of x ↦ f ( x ) + x {\displaystyle x\mapsto f(x)+x} , where f {\displaystyle f} is an arbitrary neural network module. The motif had been used previously (see §History for details). However, the publication of ResNet made it widely popular for feedforward networks, appearing in neural networks that are seemingly unrelated to ResNet. The residual connection stabilizes the training and convergence of deep neural networks with hundreds of layers, and is a common motif in deep neural networks, such as transformer models (e.g., BERT, and GPT models such as ChatGPT), the AlphaGo Zero system, the AlphaStar system, and the AlphaFold system.

explainer.lead: A residual neural network learns functions relative to its inputs rather than from scratch at each layer, enabling very deep architectures. It became famous by winning the 2015 ILSVRC image recognition challenge.

tiers.eli5: Instead of asking each new layer to redraw the whole picture, you ask it to add just the corrections, and the original is passed along unchanged.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners stack blocks of the form x + f(x) and rely on the shortcut to stabilize training and convergence in networks with hundreds of layers. A pitfall is forgetting that shape-changing additions need a compatible projection.
tiers.paperLevel: A deep learning architecture in which layers learn residual functions with reference to the layer inputs; the residual connection motif is x ↦ f(x) + x for an arbitrary neural network module f. The motif predates ResNet but ResNet made it widely popular for feedforward networks.

explainer.example: A 2015 image recognition network stacks many layers that each add a learned correction to their input, and this design won the ILSVRC that year.
